name: Windows 10 Timeline (ActivitiesCache.db)
purpose: Stores a rolling history of applications and files the user interacted with, which Windows used to present as a chronological 'Timeline', including content viewed inside those applications.
key_fields: AppId / Activity table - full executable path of the application that generated the activity
StartTime / EndTime - when the recorded activity began and ended
ContentInfo / AppActivityId - items opened within the application (document names, in-app content identifiers)
Uri / AdditionalProperties - URLs visited, when the activity originated from a browser
LastModifiedTime - when the database row itself was last updated
normal_baseline: A continuous, dense history of everyday application use (browser, Office, chat clients) with start/end times and durations that line up with the user's normal working hours and habits.
anomalies: Activity entries for an application run from an unusual path (Temp, Downloads, AppData) with a very short duration, consistent with a one-off malicious tool launch
URLs recorded for browsing sessions to malicious or unexpected domains, especially just before other compromise indicators
A gap in the timeline spanning the suspected incident window while surrounding periods are densely populated, suggesting the database or feature was tampered with
Activity for an application the user denies having run, with start/end times matching other suspicious artifacts (Prefetch, EventLogs)
anti_forensic_notes: ActivitiesCache.db is an ordinary SQLite file the current user account can delete or overwrite outright; Windows will simply recreate an empty database on next use, so a short-lived or newly-created file where a long history is expected is itself notable. Microsoft later deprecated the Timeline user interface, but the underlying ConnectedDevicesPlatform database and its population can continue running in the background on affected builds, so the absence of the visible Timeline UI does not mean the database stopped recording.
interpretation: Because the database captures full application paths, per-item content opened inside the application, and visited URLs together with start/end times, it is one of the few artifacts that ties 'what' (specific document or URL), 'how long' (session duration), and 'in what application' together in one place. Records populated by this feature persist in ActivitiesCache.db even on systems where the Timeline feature was later removed from the Windows 10 UI in a late-Win10 update, so absence of the visible feature does not mean absence of the underlying data - always check for the database file regardless of the build's UI state.
